status_summary: Measured against the call to end engagement, federal policy has combined tariff and export-control pressure with negotiated trade: a 2025-11-01 arrangement cut a fentanyl-related tariff by 10 points, suspended an export-control affiliates rule and port-fee actions for a year in exchange for rare earth and soybean commitments, a May 2026 state visit created a U.S.-China Board of Trade and Board of Investment with purchase commitments, the first Board of Trade package of reciprocal product lists was published on 2026-09-27 and 2026-09-28 (not yet operative per a trade report), and the Treasury Secretary said on 2026-09-23 that the truce was extended through 2027-01-10, an extension the White House had not documented per trade press. On 2026-01-15 BIS moved licensing for certain advanced AI chips (such as Nvidia H200) to China from presumed denial to case-by-case review with conditions. The Supreme Court held 6 to 3 on 2026-02-20 in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump that IEEPA does not authorize the President to impose tariffs, and Executive Order 14389 ended the IEEPA duties that day; Section 232 and Section 301 duties remain, including a 12.5 percent forced-labor Section 301 tariff on most Chinese goods reported in September 2026. The industrial-base goal is partly parallel through Section 232 and tariff actions, but the engagement half is materially different because trade continues under managed arrangements.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14266 raises the reciprocal tariff on Chinese goods to 125 percent.

White House fact sheet announces a China arrangement: the U.S. cuts the fentanyl-related tariff by 10 points from 2025-11-10, keeps a 10 percent reciprocal rate, suspends heightened reciprocal tariffs to 2026-11-10 and suspends the BIS affiliates rule and a Section 301 shipbuilding response for a year, while China suspends its rare earth controls and commits to soybean purchases of at least 25 million metric tons a year in 2026 to 2028.

BIS final rule revises the license review policy for certain advanced computing chips, naming the Nvidia H200: exports to China move from a presumption of denial to case-by-case review if conditions are met, including that shipments to China not exceed 50 percent of comparable shipments for U.S. end use and that an independent U.S. lab test each shipment.

Executive Order 14389 ends the IEEPA duties, including the China synthetic opioid duties and reciprocal tariffs, to stop being collected as soon as practicable; Section 232 and Section 301 duties and the suspension of duty-free de minimis treatment are unaffected.

The Supreme Court decides Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump (No. 24-1287, together with No. 25-250, Trump v. V.O.S. Selections, Inc.), holding 6 to 3 that IEEPA does not authorize the President to impose tariffs; the judgment in No. 24-1287 is vacated and the case remanded with instructions to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction, and the judgment in No. 25-250 is affirmed. Chief Justice Roberts delivered the opinion of the Court in part; Justice Thomas dissented, and Justice Kavanaugh dissented, joined by Justices Thomas and Alito.

timeline.event: White House fact sheet on a state visit to China: a U.S.-China Board of Trade and a Board of Investment are chartered, China approves an initial purchase of 200 Boeing aircraft and agrees to buy at least $17 billion a year of U.S. farm products in 2026 to 2028 and to address rare earth shortages.
The Section 122 import surcharge expires; per a law-firm alert of 2026-09-24, most Chinese goods then face a 12.5 percent Section 301 tariff tied to the forced-labor investigation.

The Treasury Secretary says in a television interview that the U.S.-China trade truce, due to expire 2026-11-10, is extended to 2027-01-10, after meeting China's Vice Premier earlier that week; Supply Chain Dive (2026-09-24) says the interview was on Wednesday, so the date is inferred, and that the White House had not yet documented the extension.

Per a trade-compliance report dated 2026-09-29, the White House and the U.S. Trade Representative publish the first U.S.-China Board of Trade package (Board working procedures and reciprocal product lists worth about $30 billion each, 77 U.S. tariff lines and 1,619 Chinese lines, on 2026-09-27 and 2026-09-28); nothing was operative as of 2026-09-29, with no Federal Register notice, proclamation or tariff schedule change.

title: End economic engagement with China and restore the manufacturing and industrial base
uncertainties: The Foreword's two halves pull in different directions in the record, so the diverged stage reflects the engagement half and the industrial-base half is only partly parallel; reshoring outcomes (manufacturing output or employment) were not measured. The title page and syllabus of the Supreme Court's slip opinion (No. 24-1287, together with No. 25-250) were read from a copy retrieved from supremecourt.gov and supplied to the project; the body of the opinion and the separate opinions were not read, and the K&L Gates summary's statement that refunds were left to later proceedings was not checked against the opinion. The executive order cites only recent events; the court_status label vacated is a best fit for a holding that the tariff authority does not exist (the Court vacated the judgment in No. 24-1287 with instructions to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction and affirmed the judgment in No. 25-250). The truce extension to 2027-01-10 rests on a Supply Chain Dive report of a Treasury Secretary interview, which says the White House had not documented it, and on the Thomson Reuters report; no Treasury or White House document was found. The 12.5 percent Section 301 rate and the report that the Board of Investment remains stalled come from one law-firm alert (Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck, 2026-09-24); the stalled Board of Investment is a status report, not an event. The interview date of 2026-09-23 is inferred from the Supply Chain Dive report, which says Wednesday. The Board of Trade package is read through the Thomson Reuters report, not the White House or USTR lists. Section 232 actions and chip-sale licensing volumes were not tracked in detail here; see c26-04 and c21-03. Whether outbound investment and capital-market limits were tightened is covered by c22-07 and c26-06. In review, diverged was kept over a low in_progress or blocked rating: the early 2025 tariff escalation was reversed by negotiated arrangements, and the latest actions (purchase commitments, a chartered Board of Trade, a truce extended into 2027 and loosened chip licensing) maintain and manage bilateral trade rather than ending it; the industrial-base half alone would rate at most a partial parallel.
